title: Chapter 92 — Ambergris
paragraphs: Now this ambergris is a very curious substance, and so important as an article of commerce that in 1791 a certain Nantucket-born Captain Coffin was examined at the bar of the English House of Commons on the subject. For at that time, and indeed until comparatively recently, the precise origin of ambergris remained, like amber itself, a mystery to the learned. Though the word ambergris is merely the French compound for gray amber, the two substances are quite distinct. For amber, though at times found on the seacoast, is also dug up in some far inland soils, whereas ambergris is never found except upon the sea. Besides, amber is a hard, transparent, brittle, odorless substance, used for pipe mouthpieces, beads, and ornaments. But ambergris is soft, waxy, and so highly fragrant and spicy that it is widely used in perfumery, in pastilles, precious candles, hair-powders, and pomade. The Turks use it in cooking and also carry it to Mecca, for the same purpose that frankincense is carried to St. Peter's in Rome. Some wine merchants drop a few grains into claret to flavor it.

Who would think, then, that such fine ladies and gentlemen should treat themselves to an essence found in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale! Yet so it is. By some, ambergris is supposed to be the cause of the whale's indigestion, and by others the effect. How to cure such indigestion would be hard to say, unless by administering three or four boatloads of pills and then running out of harm's way, as laborers do when blasting rocks.

I have forgotten to say that there were found in this ambergris certain hard, round, bony plates, which at first Stubb thought might be sailors' trouser buttons. But it afterward turned out that they were nothing more than pieces of small squid bones embalmed in that manner.

Now that the incorruption of this most fragrant ambergris should be found in the heart of such decay — is this nothing? Think of that saying of St. Paul in Corinthians, about corruption and incorruption: how we are sown in dishonor but raised in glory. And likewise call to mind that saying of Paracelsus about what it is that makes the best musk. Also do not forget the strange fact that of all foul-smelling things, Cologne water, in its earliest manufacturing stages, is the worst.

I should like to conclude the chapter with the above appeal, but cannot, owing to my anxiety to refute a charge often made against whalemen, and which, in the estimation of some already biased minds, might be considered as indirectly supported by what has been said of the Frenchman's two whales. Elsewhere in this volume the slanderous claim has been disproved that the business of whaling is throughout a slovenly, untidy one. But there is another thing to address. They hint that all whales always smell bad. Now how did this nasty rumor originate?

I believe it is plainly traceable to the first arrival of the Greenland whaling ships in London, more than two centuries ago. Because those whalemen did not then, and do not now, render their oil at sea as the southern ships have always done. Instead, cutting up the fresh blubber in small bits, they thrust it through the bungholes of large casks and carry it home that way — the shortness of the season in those icy seas and the sudden, violent storms to which they are exposed forbidding any other course. The consequence is that upon breaking into the hold and unloading one of these whale cemeteries in the Greenland dock, a stench is released similar to that rising from excavating an old city graveyard for the foundations of a hospital.

I partly suspect also that this wicked charge against whalers may likewise be attributed to the existence on the coast of Greenland, in former times, of a Dutch village called Schmerenburgh or Smeerenberg — which latter name is the one used by the learned Fogo Von Slack in his great work on Smells, a textbook on that subject. As its name implies (smeer, fat; berg, to put up), this village was founded to provide a place for the blubber of the Dutch whale fleet to be rendered without being taken home to Holland. It was a collection of furnaces, fat-kettles, and oil sheds, and when the works were in full operation, they certainly gave off no very pleasant odor. But all this is quite different with a South Sea sperm whaler. In a voyage of perhaps four years, after completely filling her hold with oil, she does not perhaps spend fifty days in the business of boiling out. And in the state that it is casked, the oil is nearly scentless. The truth is that, living or dead, if but decently treated, whales as a species are by no means foul-smelling creatures. Nor can whalemen be detected, as the people of the Middle Ages claimed to detect a Jew in the company, by the nose. Nor indeed can the whale possibly be otherwise than fragrant, when, as a general thing, he enjoys such excellent health — taking abundant exercise, always out of doors, though, it is true, seldom in the open air. I say that the motion of a sperm whale's flukes above water gives off a perfume, as when a musk-scented lady rustles her dress in a warm parlor. What then shall I liken the sperm whale to for fragrance, considering his magnitude? Must it not be to that famous elephant, with jeweled tusks and redolent with myrrh, which was led out of an Indian town to do honor to Alexander the Great?
